statement: The FX volatility smile is U-shaped because exchange rate volatility is not constant and rates jump, while the equity skew slopes downward because equity prices and volatility are negatively correlated.
explanation: Non-constant volatility and jumps (for example on central bank actions) make extreme outcomes in both directions more likely, giving the U-shaped FX smile. For equities, the negative correlation between price and volatility gives the downward-sloping skew.
originalText: The FX smile is U-shaped because exchange rate volatility is not constant and rates jump, while the equity skew slopes downward because equity prices and volatility are negatively correlated.

statement: The equity volatility skew slopes downward because equity prices and volatility are positively correlated.
explanation: The equity skew slopes downward because prices and volatility are negatively correlated: volatility rises when prices fall. A positive correlation would instead thicken the right tail.
originalText: The FX smile is U-shaped because exchange rate volatility is not constant and rates jump, while the equity skew slopes downward because equity prices and volatility are positively correlated.
correction: The equity volatility skew slopes downward because equity prices and volatility are negatively correlated.

changes.to: negatively correlated

statement: The downward-sloping volatility skew for equity options was just as marked before the October 1987 crash as it has been since.
explanation: There was no marked volatility smile for equity options before the October 1987 crash; the skew has existed only since then, which is why crashophobia is one explanation of it.
originalText: The FX smile is U-shaped because exchange rate volatility is not constant and rates jump, while the equity skew slopes downward in a pattern that was equally marked before the October 1987 crash.
correction: The downward-sloping volatility skew for equity options became marked only after the October 1987 crash.

changes.from: was just as marked before the October 1987 crash as it has been since
changes.to: became marked only after the October 1987 crash

statement: The leverage effect is the mechanism in which an external rise in volatility makes investors require a higher return, so the equity price falls.
explanation: In the leverage effect the price falls first, which raises the firm's debt-to-equity ratio and so raises equity volatility. The mechanism in which volatility rises first and the price then falls is the volatility feedback effect.
originalText: Leverage effect: an external rise in volatility makes investors require a higher return, so the equity price falls.
correction: The volatility feedback effect is the mechanism in which an external rise in volatility makes investors require a higher return, so the equity price falls.

changes.to: The volatility feedback effect

statement: The volatility feedback effect is the mechanism in which a fall in the equity price raises the firm's debt-to-equity ratio, so equity volatility rises.
explanation: A price fall that raises leverage and hence equity volatility is the leverage effect. The volatility feedback effect runs the other way: an external rise in volatility raises required returns, so the price falls.
originalText: Volatility feedback effect: a fall in the equity price raises the firm’s debt-to-equity ratio, so equity volatility rises.
correction: The leverage effect is the mechanism in which a fall in the equity price raises the firm's debt-to-equity ratio, so equity volatility rises.

changes.to: The leverage effect

statement: Crashophobia, the fear of a repeat of the October 1987 crash, is supported by the equity skew steepening when the S&P 500 falls and flattening when it rises.
explanation: Rubinstein's crashophobia explanation says traders price options for fear of another crash like October 1987. It is supported by the skew steepening when the market falls and flattening when it rises.
originalText: Crashophobia: traders fear a repeat of the October 1987 crash, which is supported by the skew steepening when the S&P 500 falls and flattening when it rises.

statement: The equity skew having been equally marked before and after October 1987 supports the crashophobia explanation of the skew.
explanation: The equity skew has existed only since October 1987, which is exactly why crashophobia (fear of another crash) is a plausible explanation. A skew that was equally marked before the crash would not support it.
originalText: Crashophobia: traders fear sharp equity declines, which is supported by the skew having been equally marked before and after October 1987.
correction: The equity skew having appeared only after October 1987 supports the crashophobia explanation of the skew.

changes.from: having been equally marked before and after October 1987
changes.to: having appeared only after October 1987

statement: For loss distributions with tails heavier than the normal, 97.5% expected shortfall can be considerably lower than 99% VaR.
explanation: For normal losses the two measures nearly coincide, but with heavier tails 97.5% ES can be considerably greater than 99% VaR because it averages the extreme tail losses.
originalText: With loss distributions whose tails are heavier than the normal, 97.5% ES can be considerably lower than 99% VaR, so the change mainly reduces capital for fat-tailed desks.
correction: For loss distributions with tails heavier than the normal, 97.5% expected shortfall can be considerably greater than 99% VaR.

changes.to: considerably greater than

statement: The FRTB 97.5% expected shortfall is a current measure, calibrated to market movements over the one to four years immediately preceding the calculation date.
explanation: Calibration to the one to four years preceding the calculation date describes the Basel I VaR. The FRTB expected shortfall is a stressed measure, calibrated to a period of significant market stress.
originalText: Like the Basel I VaR measure, the 97.5% ES is a current measure, calibrated to market movements over the one to four years immediately preceding the calculation date.
correction: The FRTB 97.5% expected shortfall is a stressed measure, calibrated to a period of significant market stress.

changes.from: a current measure, calibrated to market movements over the one to four years immediately preceding the calculation date
changes.to: a stressed measure, calibrated to a period of significant market stress

statement: The 97.5% expected shortfall and the 99% VaR are almost exactly equal for any loss distribution.
explanation: The near-equality (about 2.338 versus 2.326 standard deviations above the mean) holds only for a normal loss distribution. For heavier-tailed losses the two measures differ materially.
originalText: Because 97.5% ES and 99% VaR are almost exactly equal for any loss distribution, the switch affects capital only through the new liquidity horizons.
correction: The 97.5% expected shortfall and the 99% VaR are almost exactly equal for a normal loss distribution.

changes.to: a normal loss distribution

statement: For a normal loss distribution 97.5% expected shortfall and 99% VaR nearly coincide, but with heavier tails the expected shortfall can be considerably greater, and FRTB calibrates the expected shortfall to stressed market conditions.
explanation: For normal losses 99% VaR is about 2.326 standard deviations above the mean and 97.5% ES about 2.338. With heavier tails ES can be much larger, and FRTB calibrates it to a stressed period.
originalText: For a normal loss distribution the two measures nearly coincide, but with heavier tails 97.5% ES can be considerably greater, and FRTB calibrates the ES to stressed market conditions.

statement: In the FRTB sensitivities-based standardized approach, risk weights are set by the Basel Committee as multiples of stressed daily volatility that reflect each risk factor's liquidity horizon and the 97.5% ES confidence level.
explanation: The risk weight is stressed daily volatility times the square root of the liquidity horizon times 2.338, the normal multiplier for 97.5% ES. The bank supplies the sensitivities but the Basel Committee sets the weights.
originalText: Risk weights are set by the Basel Committee as multiples of stressed daily volatility that reflect each risk factor’s liquidity horizon and the 97.5% ES confidence level.

statement: Under the FRTB sensitivities-based method, diversification is recognized across the seven risk classes through correlations set by the Basel Committee.
explanation: The charges for the individual risk classes are simply added, so no diversification benefit is recognized across risk classes. Correlations apply only within a risk class.
originalText: Diversification is recognized between the delta and vega charges within a risk class, and across the seven risk classes, through correlations set by the Basel Committee.
correction: Under the FRTB sensitivities-based method, diversification is not recognized across the seven risk classes.

changes.from: diversification is recognized across the seven risk classes through correlations set by the Basel Committee
changes.to: diversification is not recognized across the seven risk classes

statement: Under the FRTB sensitivities-based method, the bank sets the risk weights and correlations from its own data.
explanation: The Basel Committee, not the bank, sets the risk weights and the correlations; the bank only supplies its sensitivities. The multiplier of at least 1.5 belongs to the internal models approach, not to this method.
originalText: Banks set the risk weights and correlations from their own data, and the regulator then applies a multiplier of at least 1.5 to the resulting charge.
correction: Under the FRTB sensitivities-based method, the Basel Committee sets the risk weights and correlations.

changes.from: the bank sets the risk weights and correlations from its own data
changes.to: the Basel Committee sets the risk weights and correlations

statement: Under the FRTB sensitivities-based method, the charge is calculated once at the correlations prescribed by the Basel Committee, with no correlation scenarios.
explanation: The charge is calculated under three correlation scenarios (low, medium and high), obtained by scaling the prescribed correlations, and the greatest result is used.
originalText: The correlations specified by the Basel Committee are applied exactly as given, so the bank reports a single charge calculated at the prescribed correlation levels.
correction: Under the FRTB sensitivities-based method, the charge is calculated under low, medium and high correlation scenarios and the greatest is used.

changes.from: calculated once at the correlations prescribed by the Basel Committee, with no correlation scenarios
changes.to: calculated under low, medium and high correlation scenarios and the greatest is used

statement: Stressed VaR was added to market risk capital by Basel II.
explanation: Stressed VaR was introduced by Basel 2.5 (end-2011). Basel II's innovations were credit risk weights, operational risk capital and the three pillars.
originalText: Basel II overhauled market risk capital by adding a stressed VaR term to the current VaR term, alongside the introduction of its three pillars.
correction: Stressed VaR was added to market risk capital by Basel 2.5.

changes.to: Basel 2.5

statement: Under the FRTB standardized approach, a long option position attracts a curvature risk charge because its gamma raises its value relative to the delta estimate for both up and down moves.
explanation: Because a long option gains more than delta predicts in both directions, the curvature loss is negative and so is set to zero. It is the short option position that attracts a curvature charge.
originalText: Under FRTB’s standardized approach, the long-option desk attracts the curvature risk charge, because its gamma raises value relative to delta for both up and down moves.
correction: Under the FRTB standardized approach, a long option position has a zero curvature risk charge because its gamma raises its value relative to the delta estimate for both up and down moves.

changes.to: has a zero curvature risk charge

statement: Under the FRTB standardized approach, the curvature charge for a short option position is the larger of its two shocked losses net of the delta effect, with negative results set to zero.
explanation: Each risk factor is shocked up and down by its risk weight, and the loss in excess of the linear delta effect is computed for each shock. The charge is the greater of the two, floored at zero.
originalText: Under FRTB’s standardized approach, the short-option desk’s curvature charge is the larger of its two shocked losses net of the delta effect, with negative results set to zero.

statement: Corporate investment-grade credit spread has an FRTB liquidity horizon of 40 days.
explanation: Under FRTB, credit spread horizons lengthen as quality falls: sovereign investment grade 20 days, corporate investment grade 40 days and corporate non-investment grade 60 days.
originalText: Corporate investment-grade credit spread: 40 days.

statement: Large-cap equity price volatility has an FRTB liquidity horizon of 10 days.
explanation: The 10-day horizon applies to the large-cap equity price itself; the volatility of a large-cap equity price has a 20-day horizon.
originalText: Large-cap equity price volatility: 10 days.
correction: Large-cap equity price volatility has an FRTB liquidity horizon of 20 days.

changes.to: 20 days

statement: Foreign exchange volatility has an FRTB liquidity horizon of 60 days.
explanation: FX volatility has a 40-day horizon under FRTB; 60 days is the horizon for interest rate volatility.
originalText: Foreign exchange volatility: 60 days.
correction: Foreign exchange volatility has an FRTB liquidity horizon of 40 days.

changes.to: 40 days

statement: Credit spread volatility has an FRTB liquidity horizon of 60 days.
explanation: Credit spread volatility has the longest FRTB horizon, 120 days. The 60-day horizon belongs to the corporate non-investment-grade credit spread itself.
originalText: Credit spread volatility: 60 days.
correction: Credit spread volatility has an FRTB liquidity horizon of 120 days.

changes.to: 120 days

statement: When expected shortfall is estimated by historical simulation over overlapping 10-day periods, successive trials share most of their daily changes and are not independent; this does not bias the estimate but reduces the effective sample size and makes it noisier.
explanation: Adjacent overlapping trials share 9 of their 10 daily changes. The overlap leaves the ES estimate unbiased but lowers the effective number of independent observations, so the estimate is noisier.
originalText: Successive trials share most of their daily changes and are not independent; this does not bias the ES estimate, but it reduces the effective sample size and makes the estimate noisier.

statement: Overlapping 10-day periods bias the expected shortfall estimate upward, so the bank must divide the result by $\sqrt{10}$ before using it for capital.
explanation: Overlap does not bias the estimate and no $\sqrt{10}$ correction is applied. It only reduces the effective sample size and makes the estimate noisier.
originalText: Successive trials share most of their daily changes, so the ES estimate is biased upward, and the bank must divide the result by $\sqrt{10}$ before using it for capital.

statement: FRTB requires non-overlapping 10-day periods so that the observations on losses are independent.
explanation: FRTB requires overlapping 10-day periods. Non-overlapping periods would give independent observations but need a very long history, which is infeasible.
originalText: The design breaches FRTB, which requires non-overlapping 10-day periods so that the observations on losses are independent.
correction: FRTB requires overlapping 10-day periods, so the observations on losses are not independent.

changes.from: non-overlapping 10-day periods so that the observations on losses are independent
changes.to: overlapping 10-day periods, so the observations on losses are not independent

statement: Under FRTB backtesting, a desk that exceeds the permitted number of 97.5% VaR exceptions must use the standardized approach even if its 99% VaR exceptions are within the permitted number.
explanation: A desk fails the backtesting test if it has more than 12 exceptions at 99% or more than 30 at 97.5%. Either condition alone sends the desk to the standardized approach.
originalText: The rates desk must calculate capital using the standardized approach, even though its 99% VaR exceptions are within the permitted number.

statement: Under FRTB, a desk whose P&L attribution ratios fall outside the permitted ranges in three situations during 12 months must use the standardized approach.
explanation: The P&L attribution trigger is four or more situations outside the ranges in 12 months. Three situations do not by themselves require the standardized approach.
originalText: The equity desk must calculate capital using the standardized approach, because its P&L attribution ratios fell outside the ranges in three situations.
correction: Under FRTB, a desk whose P&L attribution ratios fall outside the permitted ranges in four or more situations during 12 months must use the standardized approach.

changes.to: four or more situations

statement: Under the FRTB boundary rules, a documented intent to trade a position is enough to place it in the trading book, even if the bank cannot trade or hedge it on the desk.
explanation: FRTB replaces the intent-to-trade test with a test of ability to trade and manage the risks of the position on a trading desk. Illiquid positions that cannot be traded or hedged do not qualify on intent alone.
originalText: The credit desk may keep the loans in the trading book, because its documented intent to trade them meets the FRTB trading book test.
correction: Under the FRTB boundary rules, a documented intent to trade a position is not enough to place it in the trading book unless the bank can trade and hedge it on the desk.

changes.from: is enough to place it in the trading book, even if the bank cannot trade or hedge it on the desk
changes.to: is not enough to place it in the trading book unless the bank can trade and hedge it on the desk

statement: A desk with internal models approval under FRTB need not have standardized approach capital calculated for it.
explanation: Even with internal models approval, banks must calculate capital under the standardized approach as well, which serves as a floor and a fallback.
originalText: The FX desk’s internal models approval fully replaces the standardized approach, so no standardized capital needs to be calculated for it.
correction: A desk with internal models approval under FRTB must still have standardized approach capital calculated for it.

changes.from: need not have standardized approach capital calculated for it
changes.to: must still have standardized approach capital calculated for it

statement: FRTB requires the standardized approach for securitizations because capital under the Basel II.5 comprehensive risk measure, which used approved internal models, varied too much across banks for the same portfolio.
explanation: Basel II.5 let banks use approved internal models for securitization products, and the resulting capital for the same portfolio varied widely between banks. The motivation for FRTB's standardized approach is consistency, not conservatism.
originalText: Basel II.5’s comprehensive risk measure let banks use approved internal models; because capital for the same portfolio varied too much across banks, FRTB requires the standardized approach for securitizations.

statement: FRTB applies a higher multiplier to the expected shortfall of securitizations because internal models for them were found to be systematically too lenient.
explanation: The problem found was variability across banks, not leniency, and FRTB's response was to require the standardized approach for securitizations. The multiplier $m_c$ belongs to the internal models approach for other positions.
originalText: Basel II.5’s comprehensive risk measure let banks use approved internal models; because those models were found to be systematically too lenient, FRTB applies a higher multiplier to securitization ES.

statement: FRTB allows securitizations to stay under the internal models approach provided the desk holding them passes both the backtesting and P&L attribution tests.
explanation: Securitizations lose internal models treatment outright and must use the standardized approach, whatever the desk's test results.
originalText: FRTB allows securitizations to remain under the internal models approach, provided the desk holding them passes both the backtesting and the P&L attribution tests.
correction: FRTB does not allow securitizations to stay under the internal models approach even if the desk holding them passes both the backtesting and P&L attribution tests.

changes.from: allows securitizations to stay under the internal models approach provided the desk holding them passes
changes.to: does not allow securitizations to stay under the internal models approach even if the desk holding them passes

statement: FRTB moves securitizations out of the trading book into the banking book, where they attract credit risk capital under the IRB approach.
explanation: FRTB does not move securitizations to the banking book. Their trading book capital must be calculated under the standardized approach.

statement: When the tail beyond confidence level $C$ is divided into $N$ equal-probability slices of size $L$, expected shortfall can be approximated by averaging the $N-1$ VaRs at confidence levels $C+L, C+2L, \dots, C+(N-1)L$.
explanation: Expected shortfall is the average of VaR over the tail, so it is approximated by averaging the VaRs at the $N-1$ interior slice boundaries. The last boundary, $C+NL=100\%$, is excluded because its VaR is unbounded for most distributions.
originalText: Average the $N - 1$ tail VaRs at confidence levels $C + L, C + 2L, \dots, C + (N - 1)L$.

statement: When the tail beyond confidence level $C$ is divided into $N$ equal-probability slices of size $L$, expected shortfall can be approximated by averaging the $N$ VaRs at confidence levels $C+L, C+2L, \dots, C+NL$.
explanation: The $N$th level $C+NL$ equals 100%, where VaR is unbounded or equals the worst possible loss, so it is not an interior slice boundary. Only $N-1$ VaRs are averaged.
originalText: Average the $N$ tail VaRs at confidence levels $C + L, C + 2L, \dots, C + NL$.
correction: When the tail beyond confidence level $C$ is divided into $N$ equal-probability slices of size $L$, expected shortfall can be approximated by averaging the $N-1$ VaRs at confidence levels $C+L, C+2L, \dots, C+(N-1)L$.

changes.from: the $N$ VaRs at confidence levels $C+L, C+2L, \dots, C+NL$
changes.to: the $N-1$ VaRs at confidence levels $C+L, C+2L, \dots, C+(N-1)L$

statement: Expected shortfall cannot be approximated from a set of tail VaRs and must be derived directly from the density.
explanation: Expected shortfall can be approximated by averaging VaRs at increasing confidence levels in the tail, and the approximation improves as the number of slices grows.
originalText: It is not possible to approximate ES from a set of tail VaRs; ES must be derived from the density directly.
correction: Expected shortfall can be approximated by averaging a set of tail VaRs without being derived directly from the density.

changes.from: cannot be approximated from a set of tail VaRs and must be derived directly from the density
changes.to: can be approximated by averaging a set of tail VaRs without being derived directly from the density

statement: Value at risk can violate subadditivity, whereas expected shortfall does not.
explanation: VaR can be larger for a combined portfolio than the sum of its parts, for example when stand-alone default probabilities sit below the tail probability. Expected shortfall averages the whole tail and is subadditive, which makes it a coherent risk measure.
originalText: Portfolio VaR is \$100 versus a stand‑alone VaR sum of \$0, while portfolio ES is \$103.20 versus a stand‑alone ES sum of \$160; VaR violates subadditivity but ES does not.

statement: The standard error of a quantile (VaR) estimator depends on the left-tail probability $p$, the sample size $n$ and the probability mass $f(q)$ around the quantile.
explanation: The standard error is approximately $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}/f(q)$, so it is determined by $p$, $n$ and the density at the quantile and by nothing else.
originalText: The left‑tail probability p, the sample size n, and the probability mass f(q) around the quantile

statement: The standard error of a quantile estimator does not depend on the sample size.
explanation: The standard error of a quantile estimator shrinks with the square root of the sample size, so larger samples give narrower confidence intervals.
originalText: The left‑tail probability p and the probability mass f(q) only, independent of sample size
correction: The standard error of a quantile estimator falls as the sample size rises.

changes.from: does not depend on the sample size
changes.to: falls as the sample size rises

statement: The standard error of a quantile estimator depends on the sample size, the probability mass around the quantile and the expected shortfall at the quantile.
explanation: Expected shortfall is a different risk measure and is not an input to the standard error of a quantile; the inputs are $p$, $n$ and $f(q)$.
originalText: The sample size n, the probability mass f(q), and the expected shortfall at the quantile

statement: Holding other factors constant, the standard error of a quantile (VaR) estimator falls as the sample size rises.
explanation: The standard error is proportional to $1/\sqrt{n}$, so larger samples give more precise estimates.
originalText: The standard error falls as the sample size n rises

statement: Holding other factors constant, the standard error of a quantile (VaR) estimator rises as the bin width around the quantile is widened.
explanation: Widening the bin raises the probability mass $f(q)$, which sits in the denominator of the standard error formula, so the standard error falls rather than rises.
originalText: The standard error rises as the bin width h around the quantile is widened
correction: Holding other factors constant, the standard error of a quantile (VaR) estimator falls as the bin width around the quantile is widened.

changes.to: falls as the bin width

statement: Holding other factors constant, the standard error of a quantile (VaR) estimator rises as the left-tail probability $p$ rises toward 0.5.
explanation: The numerator $p(1-p)$ is maximized at $p=0.5$, so a larger tail probability (up to 0.5) gives a less precise estimate.
originalText: The standard error rises as the left‑tail probability p rises toward 0.5

statement: The standard error of a quantile (VaR) estimator depends on the probability mass $f(q)$ around the quantile.
explanation: $f(q)$ appears in the denominator of the standard error formula $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}/f(q)$.
originalText: The standard error depends on the probability mass f(q) around the quantile

statement: The standard error of a risk measure estimate is a measure of the precision of the estimate.
explanation: The standard error describes how precisely an estimator is determined, not its bias or accuracy.
originalText: The standard error is a measure of the precision of an estimate

statement: A larger standard error of a risk measure estimate implies a wider confidence interval around it.
explanation: A confidence interval is the estimate plus or minus a multiple of the standard error, so its width is proportional to the standard error.
originalText: A larger standard error implies a wider confidence interval around the risk‑measure estimate

statement: The standard error of a risk measure estimate decreases as the sample size increases.
explanation: The standard error falls in proportion to $1/\sqrt{n}$ as the sample size rises.
originalText: The standard error decreases as the sample size increases

statement: The standard error of VaR can be bootstrapped, but this requires a parametric distribution to be assumed.
explanation: Bootstrapping resamples with replacement from the observed data, so it works directly with the empirical distribution and requires no parametric assumption.
originalText: The standard error of VaR can be bootstrapped, but this requires a parametric distribution to be assumed
correction: The standard error of VaR can be bootstrapped, and this does not require a parametric distribution to be assumed.

changes.from: but this requires a parametric distribution to be assumed
changes.to: and this does not require a parametric distribution to be assumed

statement: A smaller sample size and a larger left-tail probability (up to 0.5) both increase the standard error of a quantile estimator.
explanation: The standard error is $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}/f(q)$, which rises as $n$ falls and as $p$ rises toward 0.5.
originalText: Decreasing sample size and increasing the left tail probability.

statement: A QQ plot of empirical quantiles against normal quantiles that is linear through the centre but curves below the line in the lower tail and above it in the upper tail indicates symmetric tails fatter than the normal.
explanation: Empirical extreme quantiles lie further out than the normal predicts in both tails, while the linear centre means the body is close to normal. Symmetric departures indicate fat tails rather than skewness.
originalText: The returns have fatter tails than the normal distribution, with a roughly symmetric center.

statement: QQ plots are useful for visually assessing whether a dataset follows a reference distribution such as the normal.
explanation: A QQ plot graphs sample quantiles against reference quantiles; an approximately linear plot suggests the reference distribution fits, up to location and scale.
originalText: QQ plots are useful in visually assessing whether a dataset follows a reference distribution such as the normal.

statement: QQ plots are used to determine the statistical significance of a hypothesis test.
explanation: A QQ plot is an informal visual diagnostic and gives no test statistic or p-value.
correction: QQ plots are used to visually assess how well a reference distribution fits a dataset.

changes.from: to determine the statistical significance of a hypothesis test
changes.to: to visually assess how well a reference distribution fits a dataset

statement: QQ plots can only be used when the sample size is greater than 100.
explanation: A QQ plot has no minimum sample size; with small samples the plot is simply noisier.
correction: QQ plots can be used with any sample size, although small samples give a noisier plot.

changes.from: can only be used when the sample size is greater than 100
changes.to: can be used with any sample size, although small samples give a noisier plot

statement: A QQ plot against the normal that is linear in the centre but steeper than the reference line in both tails, and symmetric about the origin, indicates a symmetric leptokurtic distribution with heavier tails than the normal.
explanation: A steeper-than-1 slope in the tails means empirical extreme quantiles are further out than the normal's, i.e. heavy tails. Symmetry points to leptokurtosis (kurtosis above 3) rather than skewness.
originalText: The empirical distribution is leptokurtic (kurtosis greater than 3) with symmetric, heavy tails.

statement: The QQ plot is ideal for evaluating kurtosis but cannot effectively reveal skewness.
explanation: QQ plots reveal asymmetric tail departures (skewness) as well as heavy or light tails (kurtosis).
originalText: The QQ plot is ideal for evaluating kurtosis but cannot effectively reveal skew.
correction: The QQ plot can effectively reveal both kurtosis and skewness.

changes.from: is ideal for evaluating kurtosis but cannot effectively reveal skewness
changes.to: can effectively reveal both kurtosis and skewness

statement: Any distribution that produces a linear QQ plot is a good candidate distribution for the data.
explanation: A linear QQ plot means the sample quantiles match the reference quantiles up to location and scale.

statement: The intercept and slope of a linear QQ plot give a rough idea of the location and scale parameters of the sample data.
explanation: If the empirical quantiles equal $a + b \times$ the reference quantiles, the intercept $a$ approximates the location and the slope $b$ approximates the scale.

statement: A QQ plot can identify outliers even when the other observations are broadly consistent with the reference distribution.
explanation: An outlier appears as an isolated point far from the line while the remaining points stay close to it.

statement: Real-world asset returns tend to exhibit leptokurtosis (fat tails).
explanation: Fat tails are a well-documented feature of returns and contradict the normal assumption of geometric Brownian motion.
originalText: Leptokurtosis (fat tails).

statement: The QQ plot of real-world asset returns against the normal distribution tends to lie close to the 45-degree line.
explanation: Real returns are fat-tailed, so a normal QQ plot bends away from the 45-degree line in the tails.
originalText: A QQ plot against the normal close to the 45‑degree line.
correction: The QQ plot of real-world asset returns against the normal distribution tends to bend away from the 45-degree line in the tails.

changes.to: bend away from the 45-degree line in the tails

statement: Real-world asset returns tend to exhibit time variation in volatility.
explanation: Volatility clustering and time-varying volatility are standard stylized facts, in contrast to the constant volatility assumed by geometric Brownian motion.
originalText: Time variation in volatility.

statement: In a QQ plot with empirical quantiles on the vertical axis, a steeper slope in the tails indicates that the empirical distribution has heavier tails than the reference distribution.
explanation: A tail slope steeper than 1 means the empirical extreme quantiles lie further from the centre than the reference's, which is the definition of heavier tails.
originalText: The tails of the empirical distribution are heavier than those of the reference distribution if the QQ plot has a steeper slope at its tails.

statement: QQ plots are used to smooth the empirical distribution by removing outliers through the use of quantiles.
explanation: QQ plots make outliers visible; they neither smooth the data nor remove observations.

statement: A distribution is a good reference distribution if data drawn from it produce a QQ plot that is non-linear in the central mass of the distribution.
explanation: A good reference distribution produces an approximately linear QQ plot, including through the central mass.
originalText: A distribution is a good reference distribution if data drawn from it produce a QQ plot that is non‑linear in the central mass of the distribution.
correction: A distribution is a good reference distribution if data drawn from it produce a QQ plot that is linear in the central mass of the distribution.

changes.to: linear in

statement: The main purpose of a QQ plot is to visually compare the quantiles of an empirical sample with those of a reference distribution to judge whether the reference is a plausible fit.
explanation: A QQ plot is an informal visual tool that matches sample quantiles against a hypothesized distribution's quantiles.
originalText: To visually compare the quantiles of an empirical sample with those of a reference distribution to judge whether the reference is a plausible fit.

statement: A QQ plot is a formal statistical test that rejects or accepts a reference distribution at a given confidence level.
explanation: A QQ plot is purely visual and has no formal test statistic, p-value or confidence level.
originalText: To perform a formal statistical test that rejects or accepts a reference distribution at a given confidence level.
correction: A QQ plot is an informal visual tool with no formal test statistic, p-value or confidence level.

changes.from: a formal statistical test that rejects or accepts a reference distribution at a given confidence level
changes.to: an informal visual tool with no formal test statistic, p-value or confidence level

statement: The main purpose of a QQ plot is to compute VaR directly from the empirical distribution without assuming a model.
explanation: Nonparametric VaR comes from empirical quantiles (historical simulation); a QQ plot is a diagnostic for comparing a sample with a reference distribution.
originalText: To compute VaR directly from the empirical distribution without assuming a model.

statement: In the n-variate Gaussian copula, each mapped term $N^{-1}(G_i(u_i))$ is a standard normal variable, and the joint distribution $M_n$ is the standard multivariate normal distribution with correlation matrix $\rho_M$.
explanation: Each marginal is mapped percentile to percentile to a univariate standard normal variable. The n mapped variables are then joined by the multivariate standard normal, which carries the correlation structure.
originalText: Each $N^{-1}(G_{i}(u_{i}))$ is a standard normal variable, and $M_{n}$ is the standard multivariate normal distribution with correlation matrix $\rho_{M}$.

statement: In the n-variate Gaussian copula, the joint distribution $M_n$ of the mapped variables is a univariate standard normal distribution.
explanation: $M_n$ joins n mapped variables, so it is a multivariate standard normal distribution with correlation matrix $\rho_M$.
originalText: Each $N^{-1}(G_{i}(u_{i}))$ is a standard normal variable, and $M_{n}$ is univariate standard normal.
correction: In the n-variate Gaussian copula, the joint distribution $M_n$ of the mapped variables is a multivariate standard normal distribution.

changes.to: a multivariate standard normal distribution

statement: In the n-variate Gaussian copula, each mapped term $N^{-1}(G_i(u_i))$ is a multivariate normal variable.
explanation: Each mapped term is a single univariate standard normal variable; only the joint distribution $M_n$ is multivariate.
originalText: Each $N^{-1}(G_{i}(u_{i}))$ is multivariate normal, and $M_{n}$ is standard multivariate normal.
correction: In the n-variate Gaussian copula, each mapped term $N^{-1}(G_i(u_i))$ is a univariate standard normal variable.

changes.to: a univariate standard normal variable

statement: In the Gaussian default time copula, the 5th percentile of a cumulative default probability distribution $Q_i(t)$ is mapped to the 5th percentile of the standard normal distribution.
explanation: The mapping is percentile to percentile, so ranks are preserved: the 5th percentile maps to $N^{-1}(0.05) = -1.645$.
originalText: The 5th percentile of $Q_{i}(t)$ is mapped to the 5th percentile of the standard normal distribution.

statement: In the Gaussian default time copula, the 5th percentile of a cumulative default probability distribution $Q_i(t)$ is mapped to the 10th percentile of the standard normal distribution.
explanation: The mapping preserves percentile rank, so the 5th percentile maps to the 5th percentile, not the 10th.
originalText: The 5th percentile of $Q_{i}(t)$ is mapped to the 10th percentile of the standard normal distribution.
correction: In the Gaussian default time copula, the 5th percentile of a cumulative default probability distribution $Q_i(t)$ is mapped to the 5th percentile of the standard normal distribution.

changes.to: 5th percentile

statement: A Gaussian default time copula applied to exactly two assets needs only a single correlation coefficient $\rho$, not a full correlation matrix.
explanation: With two assets the joint distribution is the bivariate standard normal, whose only free parameter is the pairwise correlation. A correlation matrix $\rho_M$ is needed only for more than two assets.
originalText: A single correlation coefficient $\rho$ is required, and no correlation matrix $\rho_{M}$ is needed.

statement: A Gaussian default time copula applied to exactly two assets requires a 2 x 2 correlation matrix with four independent correlation parameters.
explanation: The correlation matrix is symmetric with ones on the diagonal, so for two assets it has only one free parameter.
originalText: A 2 × 2 matrix with four independent correlation parameters is required.
correction: A Gaussian default time copula applied to exactly two assets requires a 2 x 2 correlation matrix with one free correlation parameter.

changes.to: one free correlation parameter

statement: In a Gaussian default time copula, no correlation parameter is needed because each asset is first mapped to a standard normal distribution.
explanation: Mapping each marginal to a standard normal does not specify the dependence between assets; the correlation must still be supplied.
originalText: No correlation parameter is required because each asset is first mapped to a standard normal distribution.
correction: In a Gaussian default time copula, a correlation parameter must still be supplied even though each asset is first mapped to a standard normal distribution.

changes.from: no correlation parameter is needed because
changes.to: a correlation parameter must still be supplied even though

statement: For two companies, the Gaussian default time copula joint distribution is the bivariate standard normal $M_2[N^{-1}(Q_1(t)), N^{-1}(Q_2(t)); \rho]$.
explanation: The cumulative default probabilities are first mapped through $N^{-1}$ to standard normals, and the bivariate standard normal $M_2$ with a single correlation $\rho$ is then applied to them.

statement: A Gaussian copula maps the marginal distribution of each variable to the standard normal distribution.
explanation: Each marginal is mapped percentile to percentile to a standard normal, and correlation is then specified among the mapped variables.
originalText: Standard normal distribution

statement: The Gaussian copula has low tail dependence, which is a weakness because dependencies, including correlations, increase in a crisis.
explanation: Because it understates joint extreme events, the Gaussian copula can underestimate the clustering of defaults in a crisis.
originalText: The Gaussian copula has low tail dependence, which is a weakness because dependencies (including correlations) increase in a crisis.

statement: The Gaussian copula is difficult to calibrate to market prices; for example, CDO tranches are difficult to calibrate with a single correlation model.
explanation: A single correlation parameter cannot reproduce the prices of all tranches of a CDO simultaneously.
originalText: The Gaussian copula is difficult to calibrate to market prices; for example, it is difficult to calibrate CDO tranches with a single correlation model.

statement: The Gaussian copula is principally static and allows only limited risk management, since it has no stochastic process for the default intensity and default correlation.
explanation: The copula fixes the dependence structure at one point in time rather than modelling how intensities and correlations evolve.
originalText: The Gaussian copula is principally static and allows only limited risk management; there is no stochastic process for the default intensity and default correlation.

statement: The Gaussian copula is limited to market risk applications because credit risk offers no way to assume pairwise default correlations.
explanation: The Gaussian default time copula is widely used in credit risk to model joint defaults through a correlation matrix, so it is not limited to market risk.
originalText: The Gaussian copula is limited to market risk applications because it requires n × n pairwise correlation parameters, which is natural for a covariance matrix, but in credit risk there is no way to assume pairwise default correlations.

statement: The Gaussian copula can be used in the default-time copula to model the joint probability of default within various cumulative time periods.
explanation: Any cumulative default probability term structure can be mapped to a standard normal, so the Gaussian copula can produce joint default probabilities for any horizon.
originalText: It can be utilized in the default‑time copula to model the joint probability of default within various (cumulative) time periods

statement: The Gaussian copula has high asymptotic tail dependence.
explanation: The Gaussian copula has zero asymptotic tail dependence, which is a weakness; the t-copula, by contrast, has positive tail dependence.
originalText: The asymptotic tail dependence is high
correction: The Gaussian copula has zero asymptotic tail dependence.

changes.to: zero asymptotic tail dependence

statement: The univariate marginal distributions joined by a Gaussian copula are normal.
explanation: The marginals can have any shape; only the transformed variables are standard normal.
originalText: The univariate marginal distributions joined are normal
correction: The univariate marginal distributions joined by a Gaussian copula can have any shape.

changes.to: can have any shape

statement: The Gaussian copula requires a single scalar (such as an average) correlation because it cannot accept a correlation matrix.
explanation: The Gaussian copula accepts a full correlation matrix $\rho_M$; using a single average correlation is only a simplification.
originalText: It requires a single scalar (e.g., average) correlation because it cannot accept a correlation matrix

statement: A Gaussian copula maps the marginal distribution of each variable to a normal distribution with a mean and standard deviation equal to one.
explanation: The Gaussian copula maps each marginal to the standard normal distribution, which has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
correction: A Gaussian copula maps the marginal distribution of each variable to a normal distribution with a mean of zero and a standard deviation equal to one.

changes.from: a mean and standard deviation equal to one
changes.to: a mean of zero and a standard deviation equal to one

statement: A copula correlation model preserves the original marginal distributions while defining a correlation between them.
explanation: A copula keeps each variable's marginal distribution and adds a dependence structure on top of it.
originalText: A copula correlation model is designed to preserve the original marginal distributions while defining a correlation between them.

statement: The purpose of a copula is to build a joint probability distribution between two or more variables while maintaining each variable's individual marginal distribution.
explanation: By Sklar's theorem, a joint distribution can be built from its marginals plus a dependence structure while the marginals are retained.
originalText: The purpose of a copula is to build a joint probability distribution between two or more variables and maintain those variables’ individual marginal distributions.

statement: A correlation copula converts two or more unknown distributions with distinct shapes into a known distribution with well-defined properties.
explanation: The marginals, which may have different shapes, are mapped to a known distribution such as the standard normal so that correlation can be defined.
originalText: A correlation copula will convert two or more unknown distributions that have distinct shapes and map them to a known distribution with well‑defined properties.

statement: A Gaussian copula maps the marginal distribution of each variable to the standard normal distribution.
explanation: Each marginal is transformed percentile by percentile to a standard normal, and correlation is then specified among the normals.

statement: The Gaussian copula is seldom used in financial models.
explanation: The Gaussian copula is widely used in finance, for example in credit portfolio default modelling.
originalText: A Gaussian copula is seldom used in financial models because ordinal numbers are required.
correction: The Gaussian copula is widely used in financial models.

changes.to: is widely used

statement: A Gaussian copula for the joint default probability of two assets maps their cumulative default probabilities to a bivariate standard normal distribution.
explanation: For two assets the copula is $M_2[N^{-1}(Q_1(t)), N^{-1}(Q_2(t)); \rho]$, the bivariate standard normal applied to the mapped probabilities.
originalText: This copula requires that the respective cumulative default probabilities are mapped to a bivariate standard normal distribution.

statement: In the Gaussian default time copula, the term $N^{-1}(Q_i(t))$ maps the cumulative default probability of asset $i$ for time period $t$ to the standard normal distribution on a percentile-to-percentile basis.
explanation: The inverse standard normal function converts each cumulative default probability to the standard normal quantile at the same percentile.
originalText: The term $N^{-1}(Q_{i}(t))$ maps each individual cumulative default probability for asset i for time period t on a percentile‑to‑percentile basis.

statement: The Gaussian copula is a common approach used in finance to estimate joint default probabilities.
explanation: It is the standard industry approach for modelling joint defaults through a correlation structure.
originalText: This copula is a common approach used in finance to estimate joint default probabilities.

statement: In the CIR model, the basis-point volatility of the short rate is proportional to the square root of the rate.
explanation: The CIR model is $dr = k(\theta - r)dt + \sigma\sqrt{r}\,dw$, so basis-point volatility is $\sigma\sqrt{r}$, which shrinks toward zero as the rate approaches zero.
originalText: In the CIR model, the basis‑point volatility of the short rate is proportional to the square root of the rate.

statement: In the Ho-Lee model, the drift of the short rate is a constant.
explanation: The Ho-Lee drift $\lambda(t)$ is time-dependent, chosen to fit the market term structure.
originalText: In the Ho‑Lee model, the drift of the short rate is a constant.
correction: In the Ho-Lee model, the drift of the short rate is time-dependent.

changes.to: is time-dependent

statement: In the Ho-Lee model, when the short rate is above its long-run equilibrium level, the drift is negative.
explanation: A negative drift above a long-run level is mean reversion, which the Ho-Lee model lacks; that feature belongs to the Vasicek and CIR models.
originalText: In the Ho‑Lee model, when the short rate is above its long‑run equilibrium level, the drift is negative.

statement: In the CIR model, the volatility of the short rate declines exponentially to a constant long-run level.
explanation: CIR volatility depends on the level of the rate ($\sigma\sqrt{r}$), not on time; exponentially declining volatility is a time-dependent volatility specification.
originalText: In the CIR model, the volatility of the short rate declines exponentially to a constant long‑run level.

statement: Short-rate models with constant basis-point volatility, such as Vasicek and Ho-Lee, have shocks of the same size near zero as at high rate levels, so the short rate can become negative.
explanation: A normal shock of fixed size can push the rate below zero even when it is near zero, and a normal terminal distribution always has mass below zero. CIR addresses this by scaling volatility with $\sqrt{r}$.
originalText: Shocks have the same size near zero as at high rate levels, so the short rate can become negative.

statement: A short-rate model with constant basis-point volatility cannot include mean reversion toward a long-run rate.
explanation: Constant basis-point volatility is compatible with mean reversion; the Vasicek model has both.
originalText: Constant basis‑point volatility prevents the model from including mean reversion toward a long‑run rate.
correction: A short-rate model with constant basis-point volatility can include mean reversion toward a long-run rate.

changes.to: can include

statement: Unlike the Vasicek model's constant volatility, the CIR model's basis-point volatility is not constant, which together with a positive drift prevents the short rate from becoming negative.
explanation: CIR volatility $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ vanishes as the rate approaches zero while mean reversion pushes the rate up, so negative rates are ruled out.
originalText: Unlike the Vasicek model’s constant volatility, the CIR model’s basis‑point volatility is not constant, which (with positive drift) prevents the short rate from becoming negative.

statement: The CIR model does not mean revert to a long-term rate.
explanation: The CIR model mean reverts to its long-run level $\theta$, just like the Vasicek model.
originalText: A drawback of the CIR model is that it does not mean revert to a long‑term rate.
correction: The CIR model mean reverts to a long-term rate.

changes.to: mean reverts

statement: In the CIR model, the drift is time-dependent so that the model is an arbitrage-free fit to the curve.
explanation: The CIR model is an equilibrium model with constant parameters; a time-dependent drift that fits the curve is the Ho-Lee feature.
originalText: In the CIR model, the drift is time‑dependent so that the model is an arbitrage‑free fit to the curve.

statement: The terminal distribution of the short rate in the CIR model is eventually normally distributed.
explanation: The CIR terminal distribution is non-negative and right-skewed, never normal; a normal distribution would allow negative rates.
originalText: An advantage of the CIR model is that the terminal distribution of the short rate is eventually normally distributed.
correction: The terminal distribution of the short rate in the CIR model is non-negative and right-skewed.

changes.to: non-negative and right-skewed

statement: Option prices from the CIR distribution of the short rate may differ significantly from those under lognormal or normal distributions.
explanation: The CIR terminal distribution is right-skewed and non-negative, so its tails differ from normal or lognormal ones. This matters particularly for out-of-the-money options.
originalText: Option prices from the CIR distribution may differ significantly from those under lognormal or normal distributions.

statement: In the CIR model, the standard deviation of the change in the short rate is directly proportional to the square root of the short rate.
explanation: The random term is $\sigma\sqrt{r}\,dw$, so basis-point volatility is $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ and rises with the rate at a decreasing pace.
originalText: The standard deviation of dr is directly proportional to the square root of the short rate

statement: In the CIR model, the standard deviation of the change in the short rate is inversely proportional to the square root of the short rate.
explanation: Basis-point volatility is $\sigma\sqrt{r}$, so it rises with the rate rather than falling.
originalText: The standard deviation of dr is inversely proportional to the square root of the short rate
correction: In the CIR model, the standard deviation of the change in the short rate is directly proportional to the square root of the short rate.

changes.to: directly proportional

statement: In the CIR model basis-point volatility is $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ and in the lognormal model it is $\sigma r$; in both it increases with the short rate.
explanation: CIR scales the shock by $\sqrt{r}$ and the lognormal model scales it by $r$, so basis-point volatility rises with the rate in both, more slowly in CIR.
originalText: In the CIR model basis‑point volatility is $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ and in the lognormal model it is $\sigma r$; in both it increases with r.

statement: In both the CIR and lognormal short-rate models, basis-point volatility is constant and equal to $\sigma$.
explanation: Constant basis-point volatility describes the normal models (Vasicek, Ho-Lee). CIR and lognormal models make it depend on the rate level.
originalText: In both models basis‑point volatility is constant and equal to σ; only yield volatility varies with r.

statement: In the CIR model basis-point volatility is $\sigma r$ and in the lognormal model it is $\sigma\sqrt{r}$.
explanation: The two forms are swapped: $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ belongs to CIR and $\sigma r$ to the lognormal model.
originalText: In the CIR model basis‑point volatility is $\sigma r$ and in the lognormal model it is $\sigma\sqrt{r}$; in both it increases with r.
correction: In the CIR model basis-point volatility is $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ and in the lognormal model it is $\sigma r$.

changes.from: is $\sigma r$ and in the lognormal model it is $\sigma\sqrt{r}$
changes.to: is $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ and in the lognormal model it is $\sigma r$

statement: In the CIR model, periods of extremely low short-term interest rates are accompanied by high basis-point volatility, which increases the possibility of negative interest rates.
explanation: Low rates give low basis-point volatility ($\sigma\sqrt{r}$ is small), which dampens the chance of negative rates.
originalText: Periods of extremely low short‑term interest rates are accompanied by high basis‑point volatility, which increases the possibility of negative interest rates in the CIR model.
correction: In the CIR model, periods of extremely low short-term interest rates are accompanied by low basis-point volatility, which reduces the possibility of negative interest rates.

changes.from: high basis-point volatility, which increases the possibility
changes.to: low basis-point volatility, which reduces the possibility

statement: In the CIR model, basis-point volatility and yield volatility are used interchangeably to measure the same volatility.
explanation: They are different measures: basis-point volatility is the absolute volatility of the rate ($\sigma\sqrt{r}$), while yield volatility is that volatility relative to the rate level.
originalText: Basis‑point volatility and yield volatility are used interchangeably to measure the same volatility in the CIR model.

statement: In the CIR model, basis-point volatility increases and yield volatility decreases as the level of the short-term rate increases.
explanation: Basis-point volatility $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ rises with $r$ but more slowly than proportionally, so yield volatility $\sigma/\sqrt{r}$ falls as the rate rises.
originalText: Basis‑point volatility increases and yield volatility decreases as the level of the short‑term rate increases.

statement: In the CIR model, both basis-point volatility and yield volatility increase as the level of the short-term rate increases.
explanation: Yield volatility is $\sigma\sqrt{r}/r = \sigma/\sqrt{r}$, which falls as the rate rises, even though basis-point volatility rises.
originalText: Both basis‑point volatility and yield volatility increase as the level of the short‑term rate increases.
correction: In the CIR model, basis-point volatility increases while yield volatility decreases as the level of the short-term rate increases.

changes.from: both basis-point volatility and yield volatility increase
changes.to: basis-point volatility increases while yield volatility decreases

statement: In the CIR model, basis-point volatility decreases and yield volatility increases as the level of the short-term rate increases.
explanation: The relationships are reversed: basis-point volatility $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ increases with the rate while yield volatility $\sigma/\sqrt{r}$ decreases.
originalText: Basis‑point volatility decreases and yield volatility increases as the level of the short‑term rate increases.
correction: In the CIR model, basis-point volatility increases and yield volatility decreases as the level of the short-term rate increases.

changes.from: basis-point volatility decreases and yield volatility increases
changes.to: basis-point volatility increases and yield volatility decreases

statement: In the lognormal short-rate model, basis-point volatility increases with the level of the rate while yield volatility is constant.
explanation: Basis-point volatility is $\sigma r$, rising linearly with $r$, so yield volatility $\sigma r/r = \sigma$ is constant.
originalText: Basis‑point volatility increases with the rate; yield volatility is constant.

statement: In the lognormal short-rate model, basis-point volatility increases with the level of the rate and yield volatility decreases with it.
explanation: That pattern describes the CIR model. In the lognormal model yield volatility is the constant $\sigma$.
originalText: Basis‑point volatility increases with the rate; yield volatility decreases with the rate.
correction: In the lognormal short-rate model, basis-point volatility increases with the level of the rate and yield volatility is constant.

changes.to: yield volatility is constant

statement: In the lognormal short-rate model, basis-point volatility is constant and yield volatility decreases as the rate rises.
explanation: That pattern describes a constant basis-point volatility model such as Vasicek. In the lognormal model basis-point volatility is $\sigma r$ and rises with the rate.
originalText: Basis‑point volatility is constant; yield volatility decreases with the rate.

statement: In the lognormal model with mean reversion (Black-Karasinski), the natural log of the short rate is normally distributed and mean reverting, rates are always positive, and the mean-reversion speed, central tendency and volatility may all be time-dependent.
explanation: The model applies a time-dependent Vasicek process to $\ln r$, so the short rate $r = e^{\ln r}$ is lognormal and positive, and the parameters $k(t)$, $\theta(t)$ and $\sigma(t)$ may vary with time.
originalText: The natural log of the short rate is normally distributed and mean‑reverting, rates are always positive, and the mean‑reversion speed, central tendency and volatility may all be time‑dependent.

statement: In the Black-Karasinski model, the short rate itself is normally distributed and can become negative.
explanation: In the Black-Karasinski model the natural log of the short rate is normally distributed, so the rate itself is lognormal and always positive. A normally distributed short rate describes the Vasicek model.
originalText: The short rate itself is normally distributed and can become negative, with constant mean‑reversion speed, central tendency and volatility.
correction: In the Black-Karasinski model, the natural log of the short rate is normally distributed, so the rate cannot become negative.

changes.from: the short rate itself is normally distributed and can become negative
changes.to: the natural log of the short rate is normally distributed, so the rate cannot become negative

statement: In the Black-Karasinski model, basis-point volatility is proportional to the square root of the short rate and the short rate follows a non-central chi-square distribution.
explanation: Those are features of the CIR model. In the Black-Karasinski model the log of the short rate is normal.
originalText: Basis point volatility is proportional to the square root of the short rate, and the short rate follows a non‑central chi‑square distribution.

statement: The Black-Karasinski model produces a naturally recombining interest rate tree, so no adjustment to time steps is required.
explanation: The tree does not recombine naturally; the time steps $dt$ must be recalibrated to force recombination.
originalText: The model produces a naturally recombining interest rate tree, so no adjustment to time steps is required.
correction: The Black-Karasinski model does not produce a naturally recombining interest rate tree, so the time steps must be adjusted.

changes.from: produces a naturally recombining interest rate tree, so no adjustment to time steps is required
changes.to: does not produce a naturally recombining interest rate tree, so the time steps must be adjusted

statement: The Black-Karasinski model is similar to the Ho-Lee model but is an equilibrium model with constant drift.
explanation: Black-Karasinski is the lognormal model with mean reversion, a time-dependent Vasicek process on the log rate, with time-varying parameters. It is not an equilibrium model with constant drift.
originalText: The Black‑Karasinski Model is similar to the Ho‑Lee Model but instead is an equilibrium model with constant drift

statement: In the lognormal models of the short rate, the natural logarithm of the short rate is normally distributed.
explanation: The short rate is the exponential of a normally distributed variable, so it is lognormal.
originalText: In the lognormal models, the natural logarithm of the short rate is normally distributed

statement: Like the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, the lognormal short-rate models have the advantage of not allowing negative rates.
explanation: Since $r = e^{\ln r}$, the short rate is always positive in lognormal models, as it is in CIR.
originalText: Like the Cox‑Ingersoll‑Ross (CIR), the lognormal models offer the advantage of not allowing negative rates

statement: The lognormal short-rate model without mean reversion is similar to the Ho-Lee model but is based on the natural logarithm of the short rate instead of on the short rate itself.
explanation: It is the Ho-Lee drift model applied to $\ln r$ rather than to $r$.
originalText: The lognormal model without mean reversion is similar to the Ho‑Lee model but based on the natural logarithm of the short rate instead of on the short rate itself

statement: In the Ho-Lee model the drift terms are additive, but in the lognormal model with drift the drift terms are multiplicative.
explanation: The lognormal tree is built in logs and then exponentiated, so drifts that add in logs multiply the rates themselves.
originalText: In the Ho‑Lee model the drift terms are additive, but in the lognormal model the drift terms are multiplicative.

statement: In the Ho-Lee model the drift terms are multiplicative, but in the lognormal model the drift terms are additive.
explanation: The two models are reversed: Ho-Lee drifts add to the rate, whereas lognormal drifts add in logs and so multiply the rate.
originalText: In the Ho‑Lee model the drift terms are multiplicative, but in the lognormal model the drift terms are additive.
correction: In the Ho-Lee model the drift terms are additive, but in the lognormal model the drift terms are multiplicative.

changes.from: Ho-Lee model the drift terms are multiplicative, but in the lognormal model the drift terms are additive
changes.to: Ho-Lee model the drift terms are additive, but in the lognormal model the drift terms are multiplicative

statement: The Black-Karasinski model produces a recombining interest rate tree only when the time step $dt$ is manipulated.
explanation: Because of mean reversion in $\ln r$, an up move then a down move does not equal a down then an up move, so recombination is forced by choosing the later time steps appropriately.
originalText: The model produces an interest rate tree that is recombining when the dt variable is manipulated.

statement: The Black-Karasinski model produces an interest rate tree that is recombining by definition.
explanation: The tree does not recombine naturally; recombination has to be forced by recalibrating the time steps.
originalText: The model produces an interest rate tree that is recombining by definition.
correction: The Black-Karasinski model produces an interest rate tree that is recombining only when the time step is manipulated.

changes.to: recombining only when the time step is manipulated

statement: In the simplified Gauss+ estimation, the long-term target is calibrated by minimizing the squared errors of observed yields relative to model-predicted yields.
explanation: The mean reversion speeds come from regression sensitivities and the volatilities and correlation from the volatility term structure; the long-term reversion level is fitted last to yields across maturities.
originalText: Long‑term target.

statement: In the simplified Gauss+ estimation, the mean reversion speeds are found by minimizing squared errors between observed and model-implied yields.
explanation: The speeds come from regressing changes in the short-term rate on changes in medium- and long-term rates; least squares on yields determines the long-term reversion level.
originalText: Mean reversion speeds are found by minimizing squared errors between observed and model‑implied yields.
correction: In the simplified Gauss+ estimation, the mean reversion speeds are found by regressing changes in the short-term rate on changes in medium- and long-term rates.

changes.from: minimizing squared errors between observed and model-implied yields
changes.to: regressing changes in the short-term rate on changes in medium- and long-term rates

statement: In the simplified Gauss+ estimation, the volatility and correlation parameters are found by regressing changes in the short-term rate on changes in medium- and long-term rates.
explanation: That regression gives the mean reversion speeds. The volatility and correlation parameters are fitted to the observed volatility term structure.
originalText: The volatility and correlation parameters are found by regressing changes in the short‑term rate on changes in medium‑ and long‑term rates.
correction: In the simplified Gauss+ estimation, the mean reversion speeds are found by regressing changes in the short-term rate on changes in medium- and long-term rates.

changes.from: the volatility and correlation parameters are
changes.to: the mean reversion speeds are

statement: In the simplified Gauss+ estimation, the regression coefficients of short-rate changes on medium- and long-rate changes depend only on the mean reversion parameters, not on the volatility parameters, so the speeds can be estimated first.
explanation: Yield sensitivities to the factors depend on the reversion speeds and maturity; volatilities only scale the size of factor moves, so the speeds can be calibrated before the volatilities.
originalText: The regression coefficients depend only on the mean reversion parameters, not on the volatility parameters.

statement: A downward-sloping implied volatility term structure is plausibly explained by short-dated volatility being currently high relative to its long-run level while volatility is mean reverting.
explanation: Long-dated implied volatility reflects expected average volatility over the option's life. If volatility is high now and mean reverts, the expected average over longer horizons is lower.
originalText: Short‑dated volatility is currently high relative to its long‑run level and volatility is mean reverting

statement: A downward-sloping implied volatility term structure is explained by short-dated volatility being currently low relative to its long-run level while volatility is mean reverting.
explanation: Low current volatility reverting up toward the long-run level gives an upward-sloping term structure, the opposite direction.
originalText: Short‑dated volatility is currently low relative to its long‑run level and volatility is mean reverting
correction: A downward-sloping implied volatility term structure is explained by short-dated volatility being currently high relative to its long-run level while volatility is mean reverting.

changes.to: currently high

statement: Returns having lighter tails than the lognormal distribution (platykurtosis) explain a downward-sloping implied volatility term structure.
explanation: Tail thickness affects the shape of the smile across strikes, not the slope of the term structure across maturities.
originalText: Returns have lighter tails than the lognormal distribution (platykurtosis)

statement: If volatility follows a GARCH(1,1) process, the implied volatility term structure slopes up when current volatility is below its long-run level and down when it is above.
explanation: GARCH volatility mean reverts to a long-run level, so expected average volatility over longer horizons moves from the current level toward the long-run level.
originalText: It slopes up if current volatility is below the long‑run level and down if it is above

statement: If volatility follows a GARCH(1,1) process, the implied volatility term structure is always upward sloping.
explanation: Because GARCH volatility mean reverts, high current volatility reverts downward and produces a downward-sloping term structure.
originalText: It is always upward sloping
correction: If volatility follows a GARCH(1,1) process, the implied volatility term structure slopes upward only when current volatility is below its long-run level.

changes.to: slopes upward only when current volatility is below its long-run level

statement: If volatility follows a GARCH(1,1) process, the implied volatility term structure is flat because GARCH volatility is constant.
explanation: GARCH volatility is time-varying and mean reverting, so the term structure is generally not flat.
originalText: It is flat, because GARCH volatility is constant

statement: When marking a book of options to market in the presence of a volatility smile, each option should be valued using the implied volatility of the most similar option tradable in the market.
explanation: Each strike and maturity has its own implied volatility, so marking with the market-implied volatility for that strike and maturity is market-consistent, whereas a single volatility ignores the smile.
originalText: For each option, use the implied volatility of the most similar option tradable on the market.

statement: With a pronounced volatility smile, all options in a book should be marked using the at-the-money implied volatility.
explanation: A single at-the-money volatility ignores the smile, misstates the value of out-of-the-money options and is not market-consistent.
originalText: Use the implied volatility of at‑the‑money options, since volatility estimation is more reliable there.

statement: With a flat implied volatility curve, the delta of a call option falls as the stock price falls and the option moves out of the money.
explanation: With no smile the delta is the standard BSM $N(d_1)$, which increases with $S/K$, so it falls as the stock falls and the call becomes less in the money.
originalText: Delta falls below 0.5

statement: When implied volatility is a decreasing function of $K/S$, as with equity crashophobia, a rise in the stock price moves an option along the skew to a higher implied volatility, so the sensitivity of its price to the stock price, ignoring any shift of the whole curve, exceeds the BSM delta.
explanation: A higher stock price lowers $K/S$ and moves the option to a higher-volatility point on the skew. Positive vega converts this into extra option value on top of the BSM delta.
originalText: It is higher, because the rise in S lowers K/S and moves the option to a point with higher implied volatility

statement: When implied volatility is an increasing function of $K/S$, a rise in the stock price moves an option along the smile to a lower implied volatility, so the sensitivity of its price to the stock price, ignoring any shift of the whole curve, is lower than the BSM delta.
explanation: A higher stock price lowers $K/S$, which here means lower implied volatility, so the vega term subtracts from the BSM delta.
originalText: It is lower, because the stock rise lowers K/S and moves the option to a point with lower implied volatility

statement: When equity prices and implied volatilities are negatively correlated, the shift of the whole implied volatility curve tends to dominate the movement along it, so the minimum variance delta is lower than the BSM delta.
explanation: The negative correlation moves the whole curve down when the stock rises, outweighing the move along the skew to higher volatility. The volatility used therefore falls as the stock rises, lowering the delta.
originalText: The shift of the whole implied volatility curve tends to dominate the movement along it, so the minimum variance delta is lower than the BSM delta

statement: For equity options, the minimum variance delta is higher than the BSM delta.
explanation: Because the whole-curve shift dominates, the minimum variance delta is lower than the BSM delta for equity options.
originalText: The minimum variance delta is higher than the BSM delta
correction: For equity options, the minimum variance delta is lower than the BSM delta.

changes.to: lower than

statement: The BSM delta already incorporates changes in implied volatility, so it equals the minimum variance delta.
explanation: The BSM delta assumes volatility stays constant and so ignores changes in implied volatility; the minimum variance delta accounts for them.
originalText: The BSM delta already incorporates changes in implied volatility, so it equals the minimum variance delta

statement: Under the Black-Scholes-Merton model, vega is always positive and highest for an at-the-money option, but these properties do not predict any particular shape of the implied volatility smile.
explanation: Vega is a model-based sensitivity of price to volatility, whereas the smile is market-implied volatility plotted against strike. A skew, smirk, frown or other shape is therefore allowed.
originalText: Under the Black‑Scholes‑Merton model, vega is always positive and highest for an at‑the‑money option, but these properties do not predict any particular shape of the implied volatility smile; a skew, smirk, frown or other shape is allowed

statement: If the implied volatility smile is a perfectly flat, horizontal line, an increase in strike price has no effect on an option's price.
explanation: A flat smile only means the same volatility applies to every strike; a higher strike still lowers a call's price and raises a put's price because moneyness changes.
originalText: If the implied volatility smile is a perfectly flat, horizontal line, then an increase in strike price has no effect on the option’s price

statement: If the implied volatility smile is a perfectly flat, horizontal line, vega is zero.
explanation: Vega is the sensitivity of the option price to volatility and stays positive even when volatility is the same across strikes.
originalText: If the implied volatility smile is a perfectly flat, horizontal line, then Greek vega is zero

statement: Vega is the first derivative of the implied volatility smile, i.e. it plots the slopes of lines tangent to the implied volatility plot.
explanation: Vega is the derivative of the option price with respect to volatility; the slope of the smile is the derivative of implied volatility with respect to strike.
originalText: Vega is the first derivative of the implied volatility smile; i.e., it plots the slopes of lines tangent to the implied volatility plot
